strengths: Addresses a genuinely novel and underexplored inverse problem: recovering dynamic 3D muscle deformation directly from multi-view RGB surface observations, bridging surface-only parametric body models and inaccessible medical-imaging-based anatomical models.

Introduces SKIM, a carefully engineered multi-view RGB dataset with a custom ArUco marker suit providing dense, temporally coherent, subject-specific skin/muscle/bone correspondences — a useful resource for the community given the scarcity of dynamic in-vivo soft-tissue data.

The decoupled muscle/skin blendshape formulation with biomechanically motivated regularizers (smoothness, bending resistance, stretch, tangential sliding, volume preservation) is a reasonable and well-justified way to resolve the inherent disentanglement ambiguity between muscle bulging and skin sliding.
Reasonably thorough ablation studies (architecture choice, vector regularization, physical energy terms) that support the design decisions and show clear, interpretable trends.

Comparison against a kinematic LBS lower bound and a recent generalizable volumetric predictor (HIT) illustrates qualitative and quantitative advantages in tracking accuracy and anatomical plausibility (reduced interpenetration, better volume preservation).
Provides an interactive visualization tool and per-muscle querying capability, which is a nice practical contribution for downstream graphics applications.
weaknesses: No direct ground truth for actual internal muscle shape/volume during motion (e.g., dynamic MRI/CT) is used for validation; all anatomical plausibility claims rely on surface marker tracking and physics-inspired proxy metrics (volume preservation, intersection ratio), which cannot fully confirm that the recovered muscle deformations are anatomically correct rather than merely physically plausible.

The method is strictly person-specific and demonstrated on only five subjects, limiting insight into generalization, robustness to body-shape variation, and statistical significance of the reported improvements.

The initial internal anatomical template relies entirely on an existing heuristic volumetric fitting method [30]; errors or biases in this template initialization propagate directly into all downstream muscle predictions, and this dependency is only briefly acknowledged as a limitation rather than analyzed empirically.

The comparison against HIT may be somewhat unfair/out-of-distribution, since HIT is a generalizable, SMPL-based, single-pose implicit model not designed for this cross-topology, marker-driven dynamic tracking setting; a more tailored or additional baseline (e.g., a simple pose-dependent skin+muscle blendshape without the proposed priors, or a lightweight biomechanical simulator) would strengthen the comparison.

Even the full model retains a substantial 10.35% deep muscle-to-bone volume deviation, suggesting the volume-preservation objective is only partially satisfied for the innermost anatomical layer; this residual error is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.

The marker-suit-based capture pipeline is costly and impractical for broader use, restricting immediate applicability outside controlled studio settings (though this is explicitly discussed as future work).

Method description is dense with many symbols and equations without an intuitive summary walkthrough, which could hinder reproducibility and reader comprehension despite deferring several implementation details to supplementary material.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: recovering dynamic 3D muscle deformation from multi-view RGB/surface observations, an inverse problem not previously tackled at this level of anatomical detail.

SKIM dataset is a valuable, carefully engineered contribution: custom ArUco marker suit, high-resolution multi-layer anatomy (skin/muscle/bone), marker tracking pipeline with occlusion handling, and canonical correspondence construction — a useful resource for future biomechanics/vision research.

Technically sound method design: decoupled muscle/skin blendshape layers with a comprehensive set of biomechanically-motivated regularizers (smoothness, bending resistance, stretch, tangential sliding, volume preservation) that directly address the inherent ill-posedness/ambiguity of disentangling muscle vs. skin deformation from sparse markers.

Reasonably thorough empirical validation given the fundamental lack of dynamic in-vivo volumetric ground truth: multiple complementary metrics (global tracking, dynamic region error, intersection ratio, volume preservation) and comparisons against a kinematic lower bound (LBS) and a representative learned volumetric baseline (HIT).

Extensive and informative ablations (architecture choice, vector regularization, physical energy terms) that clarify the contribution of each design choice and show that naive fitting without priors leads to degenerate/implausible solutions.

Practical downstream utility demonstrated via a real-time visualization tool enabling per-muscle inspection, and a clear pipeline for propagating deformations to individual high-resolution muscle meshes usable in standard graphics engines.
Honest discussion of limitations (dependence on volumetric fitting initialization, marker-suit requirement, subject-specificity) rather than overselling the approach.
weaknesses: The dataset comprises only 5 subjects, and the model is explicitly subject-specific; this substantially limits claims of generalizability and the broader applicability of SOMA as a 'parametric' model in the conventional sense (i.e., generalizing across identities).

There is no direct ground-truth for internal muscle volume/shape during motion (e.g., dynamic MRI); all anatomical plausibility claims rely on proxy metrics (sparse marker residuals, volume preservation, intersection ratios) rather than validated internal muscle geometry, which is an inherent but still significant evidence gap for the core claim of 'recovering muscle deformations'.

The comparison to HIT may be somewhat mismatched, since HIT is a static, generic-template implicit model not designed for dynamic subject-specific tracking from sparse markers; the paper could benefit from additional baselines closer in spirit to the proposed task (e.g., simplified FEM or projective-dynamics baselines) to better contextualize the improvement.

Despite framing the method as 'scalable and cost-effective,' the data acquisition pipeline requires an expensive multi-camera markerless mocap studio (120 cameras), a separate 140-camera 3D body scanner, and a custom marker suit — this is a significant barrier to reproducibility and broader adoption that somewhat undercuts the stated practical impact, though this is acknowledged as future work (markerless capture).

Residual muscle-to-bone volume error remains relatively high (10.35%) even in the full model, and the paper's explanation (a 'realistic physical compromise') is plausible but not independently verified against any ground truth, leaving open whether this reflects genuine anatomical behavior or a modeling limitation.

The initial anatomical template relies on an existing volumetric fitting method [30], so errors or biases in that method propagate directly into SOMA's supervision signal and are not quantified independently in this work.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel inverse problem: recovering dynamic, per-muscle soft-tissue deformation directly from multi-view RGB surface observations, addressing a clear gap between purely surface-based parametric body models and expensive/static internal-anatomy reconstructions.

SKIM dataset is a substantial engineering contribution: a custom dense ArUco-embedded suit, 120-camera markerless capture, careful multi-view triangulation with 2D/3D interpolation, temporal median filtering and motion-consensus outlier rejection, and a purpose-built annotation tool for resolving UV-seam marker artifacts. The acquisition and processing pipeline is documented in good detail (including in the supplementary), aiding reproducibility.

The decoupled muscle/skin blendshape formulation with biomechanically motivated regularizers (Laplacian smoothness, biharmonic bending, edge-length/stretch preservation, tangential-sliding, and canonical/posed volume preservation) is a sensible, well-motivated way to resolve the muscle-skin disentanglement ambiguity, and the formulation (including the closed-form prism volume via Gauss-Legendre quadrature) is mathematically clear.

The ablation study (architecture choices, vector regularization, physical energies) is reasonably thorough and supports the design decisions with quantitative evidence (Tables 3-4), rather than relying only on qualitative figures.

The paper is transparent about limitations (dependence on an initial heuristic volumetric template, subject-specificity, need for a marker suit, and unmodeled force/co-contraction effects at fixed joint angles), which appropriately scopes the claims.

Comparisons against a kinematic LBS lower bound and a state-of-the-art uncoupled volumetric predictor (HIT) provide useful, if imperfect, context for the proposed method's behavior, particularly the improvement in dynamic-region error and avoidance of layer interpenetration.
weaknesses: The internal muscle 'ground truth' is not derived from medical imaging (MRI/CT) but from a heuristic volumetric-fitting template (Komaritzan et al.), which the paper itself criticizes in related work as producing 'visually plausible but anatomically inaccurate' results. This makes the anatomical-accuracy claims for the muscle layer (as opposed to the marker-supervised skin residuals) largely unverified against any real anatomical reference, an important caveat given the paper's stated aim of moving 'from surface observations to muscle anatomy.'

Quantitative 'anatomical plausibility' metrics (volume preservation, intersection ratio) are self-referential to priors baked into the loss function, so strong performance on these partly reflects that the model was explicitly optimized against the same constraints used for evaluation, weakening the independence of the anatomical validation.

The method is trained and evaluated per-subject on only 5 individuals; there is no cross-subject generalization test, and the marker-suit acquisition setup is not a lightweight or widely accessible protocol despite claims of a 'scalable and cost-effective solution.'

In the main quantitative comparison (Table 2), the simple LBS baseline actually attains a lower mean tracking error (MPME) than SOMA, with SOMA's advantages concentrated in median/P90/DRE metrics; while explained via the 'candy-wrapper' rigid-collapse argument, this nuance slightly complicates the headline claim of uniformly improved tracking.

No perceptual or expert (e.g., biomechanist/clinician) evaluation is provided to corroborate that the predicted muscle bulging patterns are physiologically realistic beyond satisfying the imposed geometric priors; all evidence is either marker-tracking error or volume/intersection statistics.

The tight marker suit itself may introduce mechanical constraints on the skin (compression, marker rigidity) that could bias the observed 'ground-truth' surface residuals relative to unclothed skin motion, a possible confound that is not discussed.
